title: Vegan diet for hereditary tumour syndromes - 2
summary: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a hereditary disease in which numerous polyps form in the bowel at a young age. If left untreated, FAP almost always leads to the development of bowel cancer, often in early adulthood. The cause is a genetic mutation that leads to faulty regulation of cell growth. Currently, preventive measures consist mainly of regular endoscopic checks and, in cases of high risk, surgical interventions such as removal of the colon. There is currently no standard drug or dietary therapy to prevent the development of cancer. Inflammatory processes are also considered a possible factor in the development of cancer in FAP. Chronic inflammatory bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease are known risk factors for colorectal neoplasia. Certain intestinal bacteria can also have an inflammatory and cancer-causing effect. Data from other high-risk groups, such as Lynch syndrome, indicate that anti-inflammatory measures - such as taking acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) - can reduce the risk of cancer. This suggests that a reduction in inflammation could also have a preventive effect in FAP. Diet has a significant influence on inflammation in the body. A plant-based, low-fat diet - as implemented in a vegetarian or vegan diet - can demonstrably reduce inflammation and be associated with a lower risk of certain types of cancer. The planned study investigates whether a vegan diet has an anti-inflammatory effect in FAP patients, has a favourable effect on the immune system and metabolism and thus potentially reduces the risk of developing colorectal tumours

interventions.name: 2-week vegan diet (before planned routine surveillance endoscopy)
2-week ketogenic diet (before planned routine surveillance endoscopy)
Control (regular diet, no change in dietary behaviour before scheduled routine surveillance endoscopy)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Genetically confirmed FAP
- Age ≥ 18 years
- Ability to swallow plant-based foods
- Body mass index (BMI) ≥ 20 kg/m2 - Haemoglobin > 9 g/dl
- Normal leucocytes
- Creatinine < 1.5 mg/dl or calculated creatinine clearance ≥50 mL/min - Uric acid < 6 mg/dl
- Fasting glucose > 65 mg/dl
- Total bilirubin < 2 mg/dl or < ULN
- Written informed consent
- Willingness and ability to perform blood, stool and urine tests
    Ability to remain in daily contact (by phone or email) with study personnel to communicate important clinical information, including daily body weight, blood pressure, health status and adverse events during the diet
Exclusion criteria:
- Unintentional weight loss ≥ 5% in the last 3-6 months
- Known HIV infection
- Existing or planned pregnancy (positive pregnancy test in women, e.g. ß-HCG test in urine/serum) or breastfeeding
- Diagnosis of type I or type II diabetes mellitus requiring medical treatment
- Fasting glucose > 200 mg/dl
- Impaired renal function (creatinine > 1.5mg/dl; GFR <50%)
- Impaired liver function (total bilirubin > 2 mg/dl or AST/ALT 2-fold ULN
- Post complete colectomy
